title: The Fringes of His Ways: Job Answers Bildad
summary: Job mocks Bildad's help: what counsel has he given the powerless, and whose spirit spoke through him? Then comes a hymn to God's power over the realm of the dead, the earth, the clouds, the moon, the horizon, the sea, and the monsters of chaos. All this, Job says, is only the fringe of God's ways, a faint whisper; who could understand the thunder of his full power?
story: Bildad's short speech in chapter 25 was the friends' last word. Job now answers, and this reply opens a long section in which he speaks alone (chapters 26 to 31). Before he turns to his final defense, he responds to Bildad with sarcasm and then outdoes him. Bildad praised God's dominion in six verses; Job praises it in ten, with far greater range and depth. The point is that Job does not need to be taught that God is great. He knows it better than the friends do, and that knowledge is exactly what makes his suffering so hard to understand. The hymn also anticipates God's own speeches in chapters 38 to 41, where God will take Job on a tour of creation far larger than this one.
historical:
The chapter draws on a picture of the cosmos shared, with variations, across the ancient Near East: an earth founded over waters, a vault or horizon marking the edge of the sea, the realm of the dead beneath, and the heavens supported like a building on pillars (verse 11). Hebrew poetry uses this picture freely, as a way of speaking about God's rule over everything, not as a scientific description.

The chapter also uses names and images known from neighboring literature. Clay tablets found at Ugarit, a Canaanite city on the Syrian coast destroyed around 1200 BC, contain myths in which the storm god Baal fights Yam (the Sea) and a sea monster described as the fleeing serpent. The same phrase appears in verse 13 and in Isaiah 27:1, where it is applied to Leviathan. The word for north in verse 7, tsaphon, is also the name of the sacred mountain of Baal in those texts. Job uses this imagery to say that the powers other peoples feared or worshiped are subject to Israel's God.
cultural:
Two names for the realm of the dead appear in verse 6. Sheol is the usual term, the place all the dead go. Abaddon means destruction and is used in wisdom poetry as a parallel term for the grave (Proverbs 15:11 pairs the two in the same way). The dead in verse 5 are the rephaim, a word used in poetry for the shades or spirits of the dead, pictured as dwelling beneath the waters. Job's point is that even this hidden region lies open before God.

Rahab (verse 12) is not the woman of Jericho in Joshua 2, whose name is spelled differently in Hebrew. It is a poetic name for a sea monster, a symbol of chaos, which the Old Testament uses several times for the powers God subdues (Job 9:13; Psalm 89:10; Isaiah 51:9), and sometimes as a nickname for Egypt (Psalm 87:4; Isaiah 30:7). To say that God shattered Rahab and pierced the fleeing serpent is to say that nothing in the created order, however fearsome, can resist him.
literary: The chapter has two parts. Verses 2-4 are a sarcastic reply, addressed to one person (the Hebrew you is singular, presumably Bildad): How you have helped the powerless. The irony is plain; Bildad has helped no one. Verses 5-14 are a hymn describing God's power from the depths upward: the dead beneath the waters, Sheol and Abaddon, the earth suspended over empty space, the clouds holding water, the moon, the horizon, the pillars of heaven, and finally the sea and its monsters. The last verse draws back and makes the point of the whole: these are only the fringes of his ways. Because the hymn sounds much like the friends' praise of God, some scholars have suggested that verses 5-14 originally belonged to Bildad's speech in chapter 25, which seems cut short. Others see the hymn as Job's deliberate answer to Bildad, showing that he can praise God's power better than his friend can. The traditional arrangement gives the hymn to Job, and it reads well that way.

outline.t: The realm of the dead lies open before God
God over the earth, the clouds, and the horizon
God's rebuke, the sea, and the fleeing serpent
Only the fringes of his ways

doctrines.note: The hymn celebrates God as the creator and sustainer of every part of the world, from the depths to the heavens. The earth hangs upon nothing (verse 7) because God holds it. Nothing in creation stands on its own apart from him.
God's rule extends even to the realm of the dead and to the chaotic powers of the sea, which ancient peoples feared. Job confesses that no power in the universe can resist God.

Verse 14 is a striking statement of the limits of human knowledge. Everything visible in creation is only the fringe of God's ways, a whisper, and the full thunder of his power is beyond understanding. What humans know of God is true but partial.

words.note: Rahab, a poetic name for a sea monster representing chaos. The word is related to a root meaning arrogance or storming. In verse 12 God shatters Rahab by his understanding, which pictures his victory over the forces of disorder.

Abaddon, destruction, a poetic name for the realm of the dead. It appears in parallel with Sheol in verse 6. In the New Testament, Revelation 9:11 gives Abaddon as the Hebrew name of the angel of the abyss, whose Greek name is Apollyon, the destroyer.

Tohu, emptiness or formlessness. It is the word used in Genesis 1:2 for the earth that was formless. In verse 7 God stretches out the north over empty space, tohu. Job pictures God's creative power at work over the void.

Shemets, a whisper or faint sound. It appears only here and in 4:12 in the Old Testament. In verse 14 it contrasts with thunder: all that humans hear of God is a whisper compared with the fullness of his power.

christ: Job's hymn praises God's power over the sea and its monsters, and the Gospels show Jesus exercising exactly that power. When he rebukes the wind and the waves on the Sea of Galilee, the disciples ask who this is, that even the wind and the sea obey him (Mark 4:41). The question has the Old Testament in the background, where ruling the sea is something only God does. Verse 11 speaks of God's rebuke making the pillars of heaven tremble, and Jesus rebukes the storm with a word. The New Testament also speaks of Christ as the one through whom all things were created and in whom all things hold together (Colossians 1:16-17). The connection with Job 26 is not a prediction, but the Gospels deliberately present Jesus doing what this hymn says belongs to God alone.

hard.q: Does verse 7, He hangs the earth upon nothing, show scientific knowledge ahead of its time?
hard.a: Some readers have seen in verse 7 an anticipation of modern astronomy, since the earth does in fact float in space without physical support. Others point out that the same poetry speaks of the pillars of heaven (verse 11) and of the horizon inscribed on the waters (verse 10), which reflect the ancient picture of the world rather than a modern one. On this view, the line means that the earth rests on nothing but God's power, a theological statement using the imagery of its time. A middle position holds that the verse is not a scientific claim but still expresses a truth that fits well with what we now know: the world is upheld by God rather than by any other foundation. Most interpreters agree that the purpose of the poetry is not to teach cosmology but to lead to worship, which is exactly where verse 14 takes it.

questions: Job says that everything we see of God's power is only the fringe of his ways (verse 14). What would change if you really believed that what you know of God is only a whisper?
Job answers Bildad's praise of God with better praise. Why can someone who is suffering and angry at God still worship him so deeply?
Ancient peoples feared the sea and its monsters. What powers or forces do people fear today, and what would it mean to see them as under God's rule?
